dimension: Background job engine (lib/jobs + pg_cron tick) — performance, throughput and structural waste
summary: The engine is not starved by ordering — it is poisoned. Claiming is strict FIFO and the head of every backlogged type IS being served every tick (a job finishing at 13:00:18 today had waited 12 days 16h); the head is simply 12 days behind because service rate is roughly half arrival rate. The reason service rate is half is a single job type: `email_retry_failed` ends 226 of the last 288 ticks (78.5%) with a `started` log row and no terminal row — the Vercel invocation dies inside it, every time, abandoning every type it had not yet reached. Its handler does up to 50 serial email sends with no tick-deadline check, and each send now costs ~32s (Resend quota rejection plus nodemailer's default 30s greetingTimeout against a dead SMTP fallback), so it can never fit in a 60s function. Underneath that sits an unfinished fix: the constant-dedup-key change (audit H2) was applied to 4 SMS sweep types and not to the other 6, and those 6 hold 19,005 of the 19,007 pending rows — every one an identical `{}` payload. That backlog then makes every claim scan the whole pending set (10,440 buffers to return one row) and turns the two per-tick introspection queries into 2.1s of a tick that averages 22s. 87% of all work the engine completes is provably a no-op ("0 sent, 0 failed of 0"). Fixing the poison and finishing H2 are both small changes and together should cut pending rows by 99.9%, cron DB time by ~600,000 ms/day, and job latency from 12 days to under 5 minutes.

findings.title: `email_retry_failed` kills the Vercel invocation in 226 of the last 288 ticks (78.5%), aborting every job type it had not yet reached
findings.evidence: Live prod (as_of 2026-09-04 13:03 UTC). Per-tick last-log-row query over job_logs+job_queue for the last 24h: `email_retry_failed`/`started` is the FINAL row of 226 ticks; the next highest is `email_send`/`retried` at 14. A `started` row with no terminal row means processSingleJob never returned. Direct trace of tick 12:45 — 12:45:05.052 started email_campaign_drain, 12:45:05.632 completed (484ms), 12:45:05.833 started email_retry_failed, then NOTHING for the rest of the 5-minute window. Tick-duration histogram: non-poisoned ticks land in the 40-45s / 45-50s buckets (44+15+2 = 61 ticks, i.e. they run the full TIME_BUDGET_MS-MIN_JOB_BUDGET_MS = 40s), while 174 of 226 poisoned ticks end inside 20s (buckets 0-5s:27, 5-10s:100, 10-15s:36, 15-20s:11). job_queue for this type: 4,492 pending all at attempts=0, 1 processing at attempts=3, 895 failed all with last_error = 'Timed out in processing; reset by stuck-job sweep'. Loop site: d:\Claude\Projects\KITABU YETU\kitabuyetu\lib\jobs\processor.ts:150-163 — the `for (const type of types)` round is abandoned wholesale when the invocation dies.
findings.impact: Caps the whole engine at 4.33 completions/tick (1,248/24h) against a demonstrated clean-tick capacity of the full 40s budget. ~180 ticks/day are cut short at 5-20s instead of 40s, losing roughly 30s of work each — on the order of 1,000+ job executions/day, i.e. the engine is running at well under half throughput. It also cannot self-heal: 226 kills/day ÷ 5 attempts = ~45 rows retired/day against 288 arriving/day, so the poisoned backlog grew from 4,301 (measured earlier this session) to 4,492 during the audit. At that net rate it never drains.
findings.recommendation: Two-part. (1) Stop the bleeding now: DELETE the 4,492 pending `email_retry_failed` rows and leave the type disabled until (2) lands. (2) Make the handler incapable of overrunning a tick — see the next finding. Separately, harden the processor so no single handler can cost the whole round: wrap `await processSingleJob(job, result)` (processor.ts:162) in `Promise.race` against `remainingTickMs()`, so a handler that blows the budget is abandoned and the round-robin continues. `lib/jobs/deadline.ts` already exports exactly the primitive needed and is currently imported by only one service (`lib/services/sms.service.ts:19`).

findings.title: `retryFailedEmails()` runs up to 50 serial sends with no deadline check, and each send costs ~32s because the dead SMTP fallback uses nodemailer's default 30s greetingTimeout
findings.evidence: d:\Claude\Projects\KITABU YETU\kitabuyetu\lib\services\scheduler.service.ts:72-104 — `LIMIT 50` then `for (const log of rows) { await sendTemplatedEmail(...) }`, no import of `tickBudgetExhausted`, no per-call timeout. d:\Claude\Projects\KITABU YETU\kitabuyetu\lib\email\provider.ts:70-74 — on any primary failure it constructs `new SmtpAdapter()` and awaits it. d:\Claude\Projects\KITABU YETU\kitabuyetu\lib\email\adapters\smtp.ts:6-16 — `nodemailer.createTransport({host,port,secure,auth})` with NO connectionTimeout / greetingTimeout / socketTimeout and no pooling; nodemailer defaults are greetingTimeout 30s, connectionTimeout 2min. Live prod email_logs, last 48h grouped by provider+status: resend/failed 1,057 ('You have reached your daily email sending quota.'), smtp/failed 554 ('Greeting never received'), smtp/queued 503 (rows inserted but never updated — the invocation was killed mid-greeting-timeout), resend/sent 396. Measured cost of one send, from the 12:55 tick trace: `email_send` started 12:55:09.188, retried 12:55:41.963, duration_ms = 32,680 — i.e. Resend quota rejection (~2s) + SMTP greeting timeout (30s). 50 × 32.7s = 1,635s inside a function whose maxDuration is 60 (app/api/cron/route.ts:38).
findings.impact: Guarantees the tick kill above. Also poisons any tick that happens to pick up a plain `email_send`: one such job consumed 32.7s of that tick's 40s budget (76%) and then failed anyway. The 503 orphaned smtp/'queued' rows in 48h are an independent count of killed invocations.
findings.recommendation: Three cheap changes, any one of which breaks the 32s: (a) pass `connectionTimeout: 5000, greetingTimeout: 5000, socketTimeout: 10000` to `nodemailer.createTransport` in smtp.ts — or unset SMTP_HOST so `provider.ts:71` skips a fallback that has never once succeeded; (b) add `if (tickBudgetExhausted(35_000)) break;` inside the `retryFailedEmails` loop, mirroring the pattern already used at lib/services/sms.service.ts:1276; (c) drop LIMIT 50 to something a tick can actually absorb (5). Do all three.

findings.title: The email retry loop is self-amplifying: it re-sent one verification email 880 times in 22 hours and is what exhausts the Resend daily quota that then fails every other email
findings.evidence: Live prod, email_logs last 24h grouped by (to, template_key): `ezrawafula98@gmail.com` / `group_verification_link` = 880 attempts between 2026-09-03 13:05 and 2026-09-04 11:05; `support@kitabuyetu.co.ke` / `staff_operational_alert` = 206; `wanyonyipolycarp@gmail.com` / `weekly_summary` = 72. Only 6 distinct (recipient, template) pairs exist in the whole 24h window. Mechanism: `sendEmailWithFallback` INSERTs a fresh 'queued' email_logs row per attempt and UPDATEs it to failed (pg_stat_user_tables: email_logs n_tup_ins 47,293, n_tup_upd 44,407, n_tup_del 1), so every failed retry mints a NEW 'failed' row that becomes retry-eligible 5 minutes later. `SELECT count(*) FROM email_logs WHERE status='failed' AND created_at >= NOW()-'24h' AND created_at <= NOW()-'5min'` = 761 eligible right now. The guard that would stop this does not exist: scheduler.service.ts:71 documents the function as 'status=failed, older than 5 min, **fewer than 3 retries**' but the SQL at lines 75-82 has no retry-count predicate at all. Result: email_logs holds 42,895 'failed' rows against 524 'sent' ever, and the daily failure rate is a flat ~864/day (2026-08-28 through 09-02).
findings.impact: Burns the entire Resend daily quota on duplicates of a single email, which is why 1,057 unrelated emails failed with 'daily email sending quota' in 48h. Also user-facing harm: 394 `group_verification_link` messages were actually SENT in the last 3 days, i.e. one member received hundreds of duplicate verification emails. And it is the fuel for both findings above — without the quota exhaustion, sends would succeed fast and the handler would fit its tick. email_logs is 22MB / 47,254 rows on a database whose entire real business dataset is 9 groups and 37 members.
findings.recommendation: Implement the guard the comment already promises. Cheapest form without a schema change: in `retryFailedEmails`, aggregate by `("to", template_key, COALESCE(reference_id,''))` and skip any key with >= 3 rows in the window. Cleaner: add `retry_count` (or `original_log_id`) to email_logs and UPDATE the original row instead of inserting a new one — that also stops the table growth. Additionally treat a quota/429 error as a circuit-breaker: one quota rejection should abort the rest of the batch, not trigger 49 more.

findings.title: H2 (constant dedup_key) was applied to 4 SMS sweep types and left unapplied to 6 others — those 6 hold 19,005 of the 19,007 pending rows, all with an identical empty payload
findings.evidence: d:\Claude\Projects\KITABU YETU\kitabuyetu\lib\jobs\index.ts:111-131 gives `sms_retry_failed`, `sms_process_schedules`, `sms_poll_dlr`, `sms_release_stale_reservations` constant dedup keys; the file's own comment at :107-110 says the mpesa_*/outbox_* sweeps were 'deliberately NOT applied … not changed blind', and the three email sweeps at :62-79 are not mentioned at all. They still mint a new row every 5 minutes: `email_campaign_process` (:64), `email_retry_failed` (:69), `email_campaign_drain` (:78), `mpesa_reconcile` (:135), `mpesa_replay_callbacks` (:141), `outbox_dispatch` (:147) all use `type:${dateStr}T${hour}:${fiveMinBucket}`. Live prod split, as_of 2026-09-04 13:03: pending in the 6 unconverted types = 19,005; pending in the 4 converted types = 0 (each holds at most 1 row at any moment). Per-type pending: email_retry_failed 4,492 / email_campaign_drain 3,651 / email_campaign_process 3,589 / mpesa_reconcile 2,765 / mpesa_replay_callbacks 2,416 / outbox_dispatch 2,091. `SELECT type, count(*) FILTER (WHERE payload::text IN ('{}','null')), count(DISTINCT payload::text) FROM job_queue WHERE status='pending' GROUP BY type` returns empty_payload = pending and distinct_payloads = 1 for every one of the six — they are byte-identical duplicates. All six handlers are payload-free self-idempotent sweeps (lib/jobs/handlers.ts:23, :29, :35, :246, :254, :281 — none takes `job.payload`), exactly the property that justified the constant key for the SMS four.
findings.impact: 1,728 junk rows/day. It is the sole reason job_queue holds 84,072 rows / 35MB (11.8% dead tuples) for a system with 49 lifetime payments, and the reason every claim and every introspection query below is slow. The correlation is one-to-one: converted types = 0 backlog, unconverted types = 100% of the backlog.
findings.recommendation: Change the six `dedup_key` values in lib/jobs/index.ts to the bare type name, exactly as :113/:118/:123/:130 already do. Then one-off `DELETE FROM job_queue WHERE status='pending' AND type IN (...) AND id NOT IN (one survivor per type)`. Expected: pending 19,007 -> ~11.

findings.title: The round-robin claim predicate `($2::text IS NULL OR type = $2)` is not sargable — a single-row claim scans all 19,005 pending rows and touches 10,440 buffers
findings.evidence: d:\Claude\Projects\KITABU YETU\kitabuyetu\lib\jobs\db.ts:30-49. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` of the claim's inner SELECT for `sms_release_stale_reservations` on live prod: `Limit … -> Index Scan using idx_job_queue_pick … Index Cond: (run_at <= now()), Filter: (type = 'sms_release_stale_reservations'), Rows Removed by Filter: 19005, Buffers: shared hit=10440` — 10,440 buffer touches (~81MB) to return ONE row. The only pending-row index is `idx_job_queue_pick ON job_queue (priority DESC, run_at) WHERE status='pending'`, which does not contain `type`, so the type test is a heap filter and the leading `priority DESC` column forces a full scan of the partial index. pg_stat_statements for this exact statement: 21,233 calls, 83,258,678 shared blocks (3,921 blocks/call average, over a window when the backlog was smaller), max_exec_time 1,964ms.
findings.impact: ~5.5 claims per tick × 288 ticks × 10,440 buffers ≈ 16.5M buffer touches/day (~130 GB of shared-buffer traffic) purely to pick jobs. It is also a latent cliff: cost scales linearly with backlog depth, so any future backlog re-creates the same slowdown even after H2 is fixed.
findings.recommendation: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_job_queue_claim ON job_queue (type, priority DESC, run_at) WHERE status = 'pending';` and split the one query into two statements (typed / untyped) rather than the `$2 IS NULL OR` disjunction, so the planner can seek. After the H2 fix this drops to ~3 buffers per call, but keep the index — it is what makes the engine backlog-proof.

findings.title: The 902ms tick query is explained: idx_job_queue_pick cannot serve `GROUP BY type`, so it scans and heap-fetches all 19,006 pending rows
findings.evidence: d:\Claude\Projects\KITABU YETU\kitabuyetu\lib\jobs\db.ts:57-66 (`getDistinctPendingTypes`), called once per tick at processor.ts:144. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS, VERBOSE)` on live prod: `Sort (actual time=1593.545..1593.546 rows=11) -> HashAggregate -> Index Scan using idx_job_queue_pick on public.job_queue (actual time=4.094..1580.312 rows=19006) Index Cond: (run_at <= now()) Buffers: shared hit=10442`; Execution Time 1593.710 ms. 19,006 rows scanned and heap-fetched to produce 11 output rows. pg_stat_statements: 4,353 calls, 3,727,902 ms total, mean 856ms, max 3,158ms.
findings.impact: 246,528 ms/day (4.1 minutes) of pure DB CPU, and ~0.9s of every tick's startup, to learn a list of 11 strings. Cost is entirely a function of the duplicate backlog, so it disappears when H2 lands — but the index shape is wrong regardless.
findings.recommendation: Two independent fixes, both worth doing: the `idx_job_queue_claim (type, priority DESC, run_at) WHERE status='pending'` index above makes this an index-only scan; and merge this query with getQueueDepth (next finding) so the tick runs one introspection query rather than two. After the H2 fix it aggregates 11 rows instead of 19,006 and drops below 1ms.

findings.title: `getQueueDepth` costs 1,261ms mean and runs before any work on every tick, purely to emit one log line — 363,000 ms/day
findings.evidence: d:\Claude\Projects\KITABU YETU\kitabuyetu\lib\jobs\db.ts:89-111, called unconditionally at processor.ts:142 (`await emitQueueDepth()`) before `getDistinctPendingTypes`. pg_stat_statements: 601 calls, 757,812 ms total, mean 1,261 ms, max 2,604 ms, 3,008,582 blocks — 601 calls is ~2 days of ticks, so it is on pace for 288 × 1,261 = 363,168 ms/day. Combined with getDistinctPendingTypes (856ms) that is 2.1s of introspection per tick. Measured startup cost on live data: across 287 ticks in 24h, the gap from the pg_cron boundary to the first job_logs row averages 5.29s (min 2.43s, max 16.55s), against an average total tick life of 22s. The queue-depth query duplicates the scan getDistinctPendingTypes has just done over the same rows.
findings.impact: ~10 minutes/day of DB CPU across the two introspection queries; ~2.1s (roughly 10%) of each tick's usable life spent before a single job is claimed. The irony is direct: the starvation detector is itself consuming the budget the starving types need.
findings.recommendation: Collapse both into one query — `SELECT type, MAX(priority) AS priority, COUNT(*) AS pending, MIN(run_at) AS oldest FROM job_queue WHERE status='pending' AND run_at<=NOW() GROUP BY type` — and have processJobBatch derive both the round-robin order and the depth metric from that single result. Halves the cost immediately and reaches sub-millisecond once H2 lands.

findings.title: 87% of every job the engine completes is a provable no-op — 1,088 of 1,248 completions in 24h returned 'zero work done'
findings.evidence: Live prod, job_logs completed messages joined to job_queue for the last 24h: email_campaign_drain 'Email campaign drain (0 sent, 0 failed of 0)' ×151; sms_retry_failed 'SMS failures retried (0 resolved, 0 still failing)' ×174; outbox_dispatch ×159; mpesa_replay_callbacks ×141; email_campaign_process ×128; mpesa_reconcile ×116; sms_release_stale_reservations 'Stale reservations settled (0 consumed, 0 released)' ×91; sms_poll_dlr 'DLR poll (0 delivered, 0 failed, 0 pending of 0)' ×66; sms_process_schedules '(0 schedules, 0 campaigns)' ×62. Total 1,088 of 1,248 completions in the window. Aggregate handler time for those types over the same 24h (sum of job_logs.duration_ms): 682,610 ms.
findings.impact: 11.4 minutes/day of handler execution, ~1,100 claim queries at 10,440 buffers each, and ~2,200 job_logs inserts, all to accomplish nothing. It also crowds out real work: these no-ops occupy the round-robin slots that the poison-killed ticks never get past.
findings.recommendation: This is a cadence problem, not a code problem. Once dedup keys are constant (H2), one row per type exists at a time and the waste is bounded, but the cadence is still wrong for a system with 9 groups and 49 lifetime payments: move `email_campaign_drain` / `email_campaign_process` to event-triggered enqueue (they already have a launch path at handlers.ts:162) and drop `mpesa_reconcile` / `mpesa_replay_callbacks` / `outbox_dispatch` from 5-minute to 15- or 30-minute cadence. Alternatively make each handler return early (and skip the job_logs write) when its claim query finds nothing.

findings.title: job_logs is write-only: 449,393 inserts, 58MB, zero application readers, and 52% of rows are content-free 'Starting …' lines
findings.evidence: Full-repo grep for `job_logs` returns exactly one application site — the INSERT at d:\Claude\Projects\KITABU YETU\kitabuyetu\lib\jobs\db.ts:211 — plus the creating migration (supabase/migrations/20260526120000_041_job_queue.sql:45,63) and an RLS deny-all policy; there is no SELECT anywhere in app/, lib/ or components/. Live prod pg_stat_user_indexes: `job_logs_pkey` idx_scan = 1 (nothing reads a log by id); `idx_job_logs_job_id` idx_scan = 153,456, which matches the 149,170 rows pruneOldJobs has deleted from job_queue — those scans are ON DELETE CASCADE lookups (`job_logs_job_id_fkey … ON DELETE CASCADE`), not reads. pg_stat_user_tables: n_tup_ins 449,393, n_tup_upd 0, n_tup_del 317,090, 132,303 live rows, 58MB total. Row composition: 68,171 'started', 64,010 'completed', 87 'retried', 19 'failed' — only 106 rows (0.08%) carry diagnostic value. pg_stat_statements for the insert: 449,377 calls, 926,953 ms, 5,992,193 blocks.
findings.impact: ~15 minutes of cumulative DB write time and 6M block touches for data nobody has ever read. The 'started' row alone is 68,171 pointless writes and 26MB (index included). Two INSERTs per job also sit on the critical path of every tick (processor.ts:238 and :245).
findings.recommendation: Stop writing the 'started' row unconditionally — write it only when `job.attempts > 0` (its only real content is the attempt counter). Then either add a retention sweep (`DELETE FROM job_logs WHERE created_at < NOW() - INTERVAL '7 days' AND status IN ('started','completed')`) or reduce the table to failures only. Note the useful side-effect of keeping some of it: the 68,171-vs-64,010 gap is the only record that ~4,000 job starts died without a terminal row.

findings.title: pruneOldJobs' cleanup DELETE is a full sequential scan of job_queue, and it runs 12 times a month instead of once
findings.evidence: d:\Claude\Projects\KITABU YETU\kitabuyetu\lib\jobs\db.ts:259-267. `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` on live prod with a no-match cutoff: `Delete on job_queue -> Seq Scan on job_queue (actual time=295.644..295.645 rows=0) Filter: ((status = ANY ('{completed,failed}')) AND (updated_at < …)) Rows Removed by Filter: 84072, Buffers: shared hit=3210`, Execution Time 299.770 ms — a scan of the entire table even when nothing matches. There is no index on `(status, updated_at)`; `idx_job_queue_pick` is partial on `status='pending'` and `idx_job_queue_processing` on `status='processing'`. Real cost in prod: 48 calls, 56,213 ms total, mean 1,171ms, **max 7,851ms**, 149,170 rows deleted plus 317,090 cascade deletes into job_logs. Invocation site: lib/jobs/index.ts:340-342 — inside `if (date === 1 && hour === 8)` it calls `await pruneOldJobs(30)` DIRECTLY, bypassing the `safe()`/dedup_key mechanism every other job in that file uses, so it fires on all 12 five-minute ticks of that hour.
findings.impact: A 7.9-second table-wide DELETE holding row locks on the same table every tick is competing with, and can stall, the claim path. 12 redundant executions per month, 11 of which delete nothing. Correctness-adjacent: this is the one statement in the engine long enough to be a plausible cause of a mid-write kill.
findings.recommendation: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY idx_job_queue_prune ON job_queue (updated_at) WHERE status IN ('completed','failed');`, batch the DELETE (`… AND ctid IN (SELECT ctid FROM job_queue WHERE … LIMIT 5000)` in a loop), and give it a real job type with a `cleanup_old_jobs:${monthStr}` dedup key like every other entry in that file instead of the bare direct call.

findings.title: 100% of pg_cron → /api/cron HTTP calls fail at the pg_net layer, while cron.job_run_details reports 288/288 'succeeded'
findings.evidence: Live prod. `SELECT status_code, error_msg IS NOT NULL, count(*) FROM net._http_response GROUP BY 1,2` returns a single row: status_code NULL, had_error true, n = 72 (the table's full retention window, 07:00-12:55 today). Every error_msg is of the form 'Timeout of 20000 ms reached. Total time: 20000.587 ms (DNS time: 134.733 ms, TCP/SSL handshake time: 66.945 ms, HTTP Request/Response time: 19796.758 ms)'. Meanwhile `SELECT status, count(*) FROM cron.job_run_details WHERE jobid=2 AND start_time > now()-'24h' GROUP BY 1` returns exactly one row: succeeded = 288, return_message '1 row' — because `net.http_post` only enqueues the request, so pg_cron records success regardless of the HTTP outcome. The cron command (cron.job jobid 2) pins `timeout_milliseconds := 20000`, while app/api/cron/route.ts:38 pins `maxDuration = 60` and lib/jobs/processor.ts:72 sets TIME_BUDGET_MS = 50_000. Measured tick lifetimes reach 54.2s, so the function is NOT killed by the client disconnect — pg_net simply gives up and records a failure for a tick that is still working.
findings.impact: Extends the already-banked pg_net finding: net._http_response churn (9.3M ms / ~2.6 hours of DELETE exec time) is fed by a 100% failure rate, not an occasional one. Operationally worse, the only signal an operator would naturally check — cron.job_run_details — is structurally incapable of ever showing a problem, which is a large part of why an 78%-tick-kill rate went unnoticed until Sentry was wired up.
findings.recommendation: Raise the cron's `timeout_milliseconds` to 65000 (above maxDuration 60) so a real status_code is recorded, then alert on `net._http_response` rows where `status_code <> 200` or `error_msg IS NOT NULL`. Cheaper alternative that also removes the response-cleanup cost entirely: make the tick return immediately (fire-and-forget the batch via a second internal invocation), so pg_net always gets a fast 202.

findings.title: The 'oldest pending job never gets served' premise is wrong — claiming is strict FIFO and the head IS served every tick, ~12 days late, because service rate is half arrival rate
findings.evidence: Control check on live prod: `SELECT type, run_at, updated_at, updated_at - run_at FROM job_queue WHERE status='completed' AND updated_at > now()-'2h'` returns email_campaign_drain run_at 2026-08-22 20:40 completed 2026-09-04 13:00:18 (waited 12d 16h 20m), mpesa_reconcile run_at 2026-08-25 22:30 completed 13:00:10 (9d 14h 30m), outbox_dispatch run_at 2026-08-28 06:40 completed 13:00:13 (7d 6h 20m) — the head of each backlog is being drained right now, in run_at order. Second proof: for every backlogged type, MAX(run_at) among completed and MIN(run_at) among pending are ADJACENT 5-minute buckets with no overlap (drain 08-22 20:35 / 20:40; process 08-23 01:45 / 01:50; mpesa_reconcile 08-25 22:20 / 22:25; replay 08-27 03:25 / 03:30; outbox 08-28 06:30 / 06:35). Third proof — head age is exactly backlog ÷ arrival rate (288/day), five for five: drain 3,651/288 = 12.68d vs observed 12.68d; process 3,589/288 = 12.46d vs 12.47d; replay 2,416/288 = 8.39d vs 8.40d; mpesa_reconcile 2,765/288 = 9.60d vs 9.60d; outbox 2,091/288 = 7.26d vs 7.27d. The ORDER BY that produces this is `priority DESC, run_at ASC` at lib/jobs/db.ts:41 — within a single type priority is constant, so it is pure FIFO. The 100-190 completions/day figure is itself the ~50% chance that a type's slot in the rotation comes up before the tick dies on email_retry_failed (rotateStartingType, processor.ts:228-233, is the only reason it is 50% rather than 0%).
findings.impact: Matters because it redirects the fix. No amount of further scheduler-fairness work (a fourth round of the August incident's fixes) will help: fairness is already correct. The two levers that actually move the number are (a) stop the tick from dying, and (b) stop enqueuing 288 duplicates/day per type. Both are elsewhere in this list and both are small.
findings.recommendation: Do not add another priority/fairness mechanism. Treat oldest-pending-age as `backlog ÷ arrival rate` and drive it down by cutting the backlog (H2) rather than by re-ordering claims. Add an assertion to the starvation detector so it distinguishes the two cases: report `oldest_mins` alongside `completions_in_window` per type — a type completing >0 with a large oldest_mins is a throughput deficit, a type completing 0 is a genuine stall.

findings.title: Re-design: the fixes compound — pending 19,007 -> ~11, ~610,000 ms/day of DB time and ~130 GB/day of buffer traffic removed, job latency 12 days -> under 5 minutes
findings.evidence: All inputs measured above on live prod at 2026-09-04 13:03 UTC. Current steady state: 288 ticks/day, 4.33 completions/tick (1,248/day) of which 1,088 are no-ops; average tick life 22.0s (5.29s startup + 16.74s work window); 226/288 ticks killed. Ceiling proof that the budget, not the design, is the binding constraint once the poison is gone: the 61 non-poisoned ticks all land in the 40-50s duration buckets, i.e. they exit on `TIME_BUDGET_MS - MIN_JOB_BUDGET_MS` (processor.ts:152) exactly as designed. Measured per-job overhead between completions in the clean 12:55 trace is a consistent 0.197-0.208s (markJobCompleted + 2 logJob + 1 claim), and every non-email handler completes in 384-1,008 ms.
findings.impact: Ordered by leverage per line changed: (1) constant dedup_key on the 6 types — 6 one-line edits, removes 19,004 rows and 1,728 junk enqueues/day; this alone takes getDistinctPendingTypes from 856ms to sub-ms (-246,528 ms/day), getQueueDepth from 1,261ms to sub-ms (-363,168 ms/day), and each claim from 10,440 buffers to ~3 (-130 GB/day of buffer traffic). (2) SMTP timeouts + deadline check in retryFailedEmails — restores ~180 ticks/day from a 5-20s death to the full 40s window. (3) retry-count guard — stops the Resend quota exhaustion and the email_logs growth. (4) idx_job_queue_claim — makes (1) durable against any future backlog.
